examples.title: Diagnosing Why northfield-orders-etl Suddenly Reprocessed a Year of History
examples.context: Lesson 5 explains why job bookmarks matter in the abstract: without them, every run reprocesses the entire raw zone instead of just new data. This worked example is the real incident that explanation predicts — a routine-looking change to northfield-orders-etl silently resets its bookmark, and the next run's DPU bill (and runtime) spikes without any error being thrown.
examples.objective: Given a Glue job run that took 40x longer and cost far more than usual, with no error in the logs, determine why job bookmarks stopped working and fix it without permanently losing bookmark tracking going forward.
examples.startingInformation: **The symptom:** last night's `northfield-orders-etl` run took 3 hours and processed 400 million rows, instead of its usual 90 seconds and ~50,000 rows for one night's partition. The job succeeded — no error, no failed state in Step Functions. **What changed recently:** a teammate refactored the script yesterday, renaming the `transformation_ctx` parameter on the `create_dynamic_frame.from_catalog` call from `"raw_orders"` to `"orders_source"` as part of a general cleanup pass, and also updated the Glue job's `--JOB_NAME` argument's underlying job name slightly for consistency with the new naming convention from Lesson 2.
examples.walkthrough:
**Step 1 — Confirm what actually ran, using CloudWatch (Chapter 3's monitoring lessons).** The job's CloudWatch metrics confirm 400M rows processed, matching the full historical volume of `northfield_orders_raw` to date — not one night's incremental partition. This rules out a data volume spike on the source side; the job genuinely reprocessed everything.

**Step 2 — Check whether bookmarks are even still enabled.** `aws glue get-job --job-name northfield-orders-etl` confirms `JobBookmark.Enabled` is still `true` in the job's own configuration — so this isn't a case of someone explicitly disabling bookmarks. The setting is correct; something else broke the mechanism.

**Step 3 — Recall exactly what a bookmark actually tracks.** Lesson 5 states bookmarks track "which S3 objects Glue has already processed" — but the specific mechanism ties that tracking to the `transformation_ctx` string passed into the read call, combined with the job's own name. Both of those are effectively part of the bookmark's identity, not just labels.

**Step 4 — Connect the dots to yesterday's refactor.** Changing `transformation_ctx` from `"raw_orders"` to `"orders_source"` means Glue's bookmark state — which was keyed to the old context string — no longer matches anything the job is currently asking about. From the bookmark system's point of view, this looks like a brand-new read operation with no prior history, so it defaults to "nothing has ever been processed" and reads everything.
examples.reasoning: The actual lesson here isn't "don't rename things" — code does get refactored, and `transformation_ctx` naming genuinely can and should improve over time. The lesson is that **a bookmark's identity is tied to specific strings in the code, not just to the job as a whole**, which makes it a surprisingly fragile thing to refactor casually. A rename that looks purely cosmetic (just a clearer parameter name) is, to the bookmark system, indistinguishable from pointing at an entirely different data read. This is exactly the kind of gotcha that doesn't show up in a quick local test (which naturally doesn't have bookmark history to break) and only surfaces on the next real incremental run in production — which is precisely what happened here.
examples.solution:
```python
# What changed (looks cosmetic, isn't):
# Before:
raw = glueContext.create_dynamic_frame.from_catalog(
    database="northfield_catalog",
    table_name="northfield_orders_raw",
    transformation_ctx="raw_orders",  # <- bookmark state keyed to this string
)

# After yesterday's refactor:
raw = glueContext.create_dynamic_frame.from_catalog(
    database="northfield_catalog",
    table_name="northfield_orders_raw",
    transformation_ctx="orders_source",  # <- no bookmark history exists for this string
)
```

```text
-- Immediate fix: there is no way to "merge" bookmark history onto a
-- new transformation_ctx. The practical options are:
--
-- Option A (if a one-time full reprocess is actually fine, and
-- dropUpsert/overwrite semantics in the target won't create
-- duplicates): accept last night's full run as a one-time cost,
-- and let the bookmark build fresh history from here under the new
-- transformation_ctx name going forward.
--
-- Option B (if the target table can't safely absorb a full
-- reprocess, e.g. it would double-count via an append-only write):
-- revert transformation_ctx back to the original "raw_orders" string
-- specifically, so existing bookmark history is recognized again,
-- and defer the naming cleanup to a deliberate, planned migration
-- instead of a routine refactor.
```

```bash
# Confirm which situation applies before choosing:
aws glue get-job-bookmark --job-name northfield-orders-etl
# Inspect the bookmark's recorded state directly rather than guessing
```
examples.validation: After applying the fix, run the job against a single new day's partition and confirm via CloudWatch metrics that it processes only that partition's row count, not the full historical volume. Confirm the job's duration and DPU-hours return to the normal ~90-second baseline from Lesson 12's cost discussion. If Option B was used, confirm with a teammate that any future `transformation_ctx` renaming is treated as a deliberate, planned change — not a routine refactor — going forward.
examples.pitfalls:
- **Assuming a renamed parameter is purely cosmetic** without checking whether that exact string is load-bearing for a stateful mechanism like bookmarks.
- **Disabling bookmarks entirely "to be safe"** after an incident like this — that doesn't fix the underlying issue, it just makes every future run reprocess everything on purpose instead of by accident.
- **Assuming the job succeeding (no error, no Step Functions failure) means nothing went wrong.** A silently-reset bookmark produces a correct result at a dramatically higher cost — exactly the kind of incident that doesn't trip an error-based alert and needs a cost/duration-based one instead.

examples.title: Migrating Northfield's Curated Zone to Iceberg via S3 Tables
examples.context: Lesson 5 writes the curated zone as plain partitioned Parquet, which was the right, simple choice for a capstone-scale nightly batch job. This worked example asks a realistic follow-up question an interviewer might actually pose: what would change if Northfield's analysts started needing to correct individual bad order records after the fact, not just wait for tomorrow's full reprocessing run?
examples.objective: Identify why plain partitioned Parquet makes row-level correction genuinely painful, and redesign the curated zone's write path to use Iceberg via S3 Tables instead, without changing the Glue ETL job's core transformation logic from Lesson 5.
examples.startingInformation:
**The new requirement:** Northfield's analysts occasionally discover a single bad order record (a data-entry error at the source) that needs correcting in `northfield_orders_curated` without waiting for the next scheduled reprocessing run, and without risking Athena/Redshift queries seeing a half-updated result while the fix is applied. **The current write path**, from Lesson 5:

```python
curated.write.mode("append").partitionBy("dt").parquet(
    "s3://northfield-curated-zone/orders/"
)
```
examples.walkthrough:
**Step 1 — Name the actual limitation, using this course's own new Chapter 12 material.** Plain partitioned Parquet has no concept of a row-level update — correcting one bad order inside a `dt=2026-06-15` partition means rewriting that entire partition's files, and there's no safe way for a concurrent Athena query to avoid seeing a partially-rewritten partition mid-operation. This is precisely the gap Chapter 12's Iceberg lesson describes.

**Step 2 — Decide between the two real Iceberg paths from Chapter 12: self-managed Glue tables, or S3 Tables.** Northfield's team is small, with no dedicated platform engineer to run and monitor periodic compaction/snapshot-expiration jobs — which points toward S3 Tables specifically, since AWS handles that maintenance automatically, rather than the classic Glue-managed Iceberg path that would add a new operational responsibility this team doesn't have capacity for.

**Step 3 — Change the write path, keeping Lesson 5's transformation logic untouched.** The `.withColumn(...)` cleaning steps don't change at all — only the final write call changes from a Parquet file write to an Iceberg table write/merge, targeting a table registered in an S3 Tables bucket.

**Step 4 — Confirm nothing downstream breaks.** Athena (Lesson 7) and Redshift (Lesson 6) both already query through the Glue Data Catalog — since S3 Tables integrates with the Catalog directly, neither downstream query needs to change at all, as long as the table is registered under the same `northfield_catalog.northfield_orders_curated` name analysts and reports already reference.
examples.reasoning: The choice in Step 2 — S3 Tables over self-managed Glue-based Iceberg — is the one worth defending explicitly in an interview, and it's a real trade-off, not an obvious default. Self-managed Iceberg on a general-purpose bucket gives more control (you can tune compaction scheduling precisely to your own workload), but it adds an operational surface area: someone has to own, monitor, and alert on those maintenance jobs. For a small team already running lean (this capstone has no dedicated platform role), S3 Tables' automatic maintenance converts a new operational burden into something AWS handles — the right trade-off for *this* team's actual size and capacity, which is exactly the kind of context-specific reasoning Lesson 14's "what would you do differently" interview question is looking for, rather than a generic "we'd use Iceberg" answer with no justification for which flavor.
examples.solution:
```python
# Lesson 5's cleaning logic is completely unchanged:
curated = (
    raw
    .withColumn("order_date", to_date(col("order_date"), "yyyy-MM-dd"))
    .withColumn("region", upper(trim(col("region"))))
    .withColumn("quantity", col("quantity").cast("int"))
    .withColumn("unit_price", col("unit_price").cast("decimal(10,2)"))
    .withColumn("order_total", col("quantity") * col("unit_price"))
    .dropDuplicates(["order_id"])
    .filter(col("order_id").isNotNull())
)

# Only the write path changes -- from a Parquet file write to an
# Iceberg table write, against a table registered in an S3 Tables
# bucket integrated with northfield_catalog.
curated.createOrReplaceTempView("curated_batch")

spark.sql("""
    MERGE INTO glue_catalog.northfield_catalog.northfield_orders_curated t
    USING curated_batch s
    ON t.order_id = s.order_id
    WHEN MATCHED THEN UPDATE SET *
    WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT *
""")
```

```text
-- The analyst's one-off correction, now possible without a full
-- reprocessing run and without any downstream query risk:
UPDATE glue_catalog.northfield_catalog.northfield_orders_curated
SET quantity = 12
WHERE order_id = 'ORD-48213';
-- Athena/Redshift readers see either the pre- or post-correction
-- snapshot, never a half-written intermediate state.
```
examples.validation: Run the migrated job against a test partition and confirm the output table is registered correctly in `northfield_catalog` with the same name Athena/Redshift already query. Perform a single-row correction via `UPDATE` and confirm, by querying before and after from a separate session, that readers never see a partial or inconsistent result mid-update. Confirm the nightly incremental job (with job bookmarks, per Worked Example 1's lesson) still only processes new partitions, now merging into the Iceberg table instead of appending new Parquet files.
examples.pitfalls:
- **Rewriting the Lesson 5 transformation logic unnecessarily** — the actual change is scoped entirely to the write path; the cleaning steps that already work don't need to be touched.
- **Choosing self-managed Iceberg out of habit without weighing the new operational burden** against the team's actual size and capacity — the "more control" option isn't automatically the right one.
- **Forgetting that a MERGE needs a matching key** (`order_id` here) — without one, the write degrades into something closer to a plain append, losing the row-level correction capability this migration was for in the first place.

examples.title: Locking Down a New PII Column With Lake Formation, Without Breaking Existing Analysts
examples.context: Lesson 10 writes least-privilege IAM roles scoped to whole tables and buckets — real, resource-level ARNs, exactly right for service-to-service access. It doesn't address a different, realistic request: restricting one specific column from one specific group of human analysts, while every other analyst and every existing query keeps working unchanged. This worked example picks up exactly where Lesson 10 leaves off, using Chapter 12's new Lake Formation material.
examples.objective: Given a new requirement to add a customer email column to northfield_orders_curated that only a small Compliance group should be able to see, restrict access to that one column without disrupting the broader analyst team's existing table-level access.
examples.startingInformation: **The new requirement:** `northfield_orders_curated` is getting a new `customer_email` column. Most of Northfield's analyst team should keep querying the table exactly as before; only a 3-person Compliance group should be able to see the new column. **What already exists, from Lesson 10:** IAM roles scoped at the table/bucket level (`northfield-redshift-copy-role`, etc.) — none of which have any concept of per-column restriction, because that's not what IAM is for.
examples.walkthrough:
**Step 1 — Recognize this is explicitly a Lake Formation problem, not an IAM problem (Chapter 12).** Lesson 10's roles already correctly grant table-level read access to the services and roles that need it. Restricting one new column from a subset of *human* analysts who otherwise share a role or group is exactly the gap Chapter 12 describes IAM as unable to express on its own.

**Step 2 — Confirm the account isn't running Lake Formation's default 'Open' method first**, per Chapter 12 — if it is, any column-level grant written in Step 3 would be silently bypassed by `Super` permission on `IAMAllowedPrincipals`, and the fix would appear not to work for a reason that has nothing to do with the grant itself.

**Step 3 — Tag the new column**, rather than writing a one-off grant naming this specific column — consistent with the LF-Tags approach from Chapter 12, which pays off the next time a similarly sensitive column gets added.

**Step 4 — Grant the Compliance group access to the `sensitivity=pii` tag, and confirm the broader analyst group's existing access is untouched** — no change needed to their existing grants at all, since nothing about restricting a new column should require re-granting access to columns that already worked.
examples.reasoning:
Step 2 is the step most likely to get skipped under time pressure, and skipping it produces a confusing debugging experience: the grant will look syntactically correct, and will still not work, for a reason that's easy to misdiagnose as "I wrote the grant wrong" when the real cause is an account-level setting from before Lake Formation was ever introduced to this project. This is exactly the kind of gotcha Chapter 12 flags explicitly, and it's worth checking first, before spending time re-writing a grant that was never the actual problem.

The choice to tag the column (Step 3) rather than grant access to the specific column name directly is the same reasoning Chapter 12 gives for LF-Tags generally: the next sensitive column Northfield adds — a phone number, a billing address — can reuse the same `sensitivity=pii` tag and the same Compliance grant, with no new grant needed.
examples.solution:
```bash
# Step 2: confirm Lake Formation isn't running the default Open method
aws lakeformation get-data-lake-settings
# Check that IAMAllowedPrincipals doesn't have blanket Super access
# on northfield_catalog -- if it does, this has to be addressed
# first, or the grant below will appear to do nothing.

# Step 3: tag the new column
aws lakeformation add-lf-tags-to-resource \
  --resource '{"TableWithColumns":{"DatabaseName":"northfield_catalog","Name":"northfield_orders_curated","ColumnNames":["customer_email"]}}' \
  --lf-tags '[{"CatalogId":"111122223333","TagKey":"sensitivity","TagValues":["pii"]}]'

# Step 4: grant the Compliance group access via the tag
aws lakeformation grant-permissions \
  --principal DataLakePrincipalIdentifier=arn:aws:iam::111122223333:role/northfield-compliance-group \
  --resource '{"LFTagPolicy":{"ResourceType":"TABLE","Expression":[{"TagKey":"sensitivity","TagValues":["pii"]}]}}' \
  --permissions SELECT DESCRIBE

# No change needed to the broader analyst role's existing grants --
# they were never granted access to this column in the first place,
# so there's nothing to revoke; they simply never see it.
```
examples.validation: Query `northfield_orders_curated` as a member of the broader analyst group and confirm `customer_email` either doesn't appear or returns no data, while every other column returns normally, unchanged from before this column existed. Query the same table as a Compliance group member and confirm `customer_email` returns real data. Add a second, unrelated sensitive column later and confirm tagging it `sensitivity=pii` is sufficient — no new grant required for the Compliance group to see it too.
examples.pitfalls:
- **Writing the column-level grant without first checking the account's Lake Formation access-control method** — produces a grant that looks right and silently doesn't work.
- **Granting access to the specific column name instead of a reusable tag**, recreating the same manual-grant toil for every future sensitive column added later.
- **Assuming the broader analyst group's access needs to be explicitly re-confirmed or re-granted** — if they never had access to the new column, there's nothing to change about their existing grants at all.
